newsitem.title: INDIA: Wives of Kashmir hostages torn by uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Wives of Kashmir hostages torn by uncertainty.

text.p: The wives of two Western tourists kidnapped in Kashmir two years ago said on Thursday they did not know if their husbands were dead or alive, but they had returned to India for answers to their haunting questions.

Julie Mangan, wife of Briton Keith Mangan, and Jane Schelly, wife of American Donald Hutchings, said they were dismayed that there had been no reliable news on their husbands for more than a year, but that they had not given up hope.

"It is discouraging and certainly it is not a positive sign," Schelly told Reuters in an interview. "It's frustrating and a very bad sign to us. Why haven't there been communications, requests, demands?
"If they are alive, why has there been no contact? But if they've been killed, why has that not been brought out either?"
Keith Mangan and Donald Hutchings were kidnapped by Al-Faran guerrillas on July 4, 1995, while trekking in the mountains of south Kashmir with American John Childs and Briton Paul Wells.

Four days later, Childs escaped to freedom and the shadowy militants captured German Dirk Hasert and Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe. Five weeks later, the Norwegian was found beheaded in a remote Kashmiri forest.

Both Julie Mangan and Jane Schelly were with their husbands when the men were captured but were allowed to go free. They have returned to Kashmir several times since and in coming days will press local officials and separatists for information.
"We just want to make sure than they (officials) carry on until we find the answer," Julie Mangan said. "It's very little to ask, just to know their whereabouts."

Last December the Indian government offered a one-million-rupee ($28,000) reward for information about the hostages. Authorities in Srinagar, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, say no one has yet offered any tip-offs.
"I'm not surprised. It's very frightening for people to come forward," Julie Mangan said.

"Somewhere, somebody knows," Schelly said. "You cannot keep secrets in the Kashmir Valley. People know things. If they were killed, somebody would know. And likewise if the hostages are alive, people would also know that."

In the past year, two captured militants from Pakistan-based Harkat-ul-Ansar outfit have said they were told that the four hostages were shot and buried in a remote forest in south Kashmir. India says Harkat-ul-Ansar is linked to Al-Faran.

Local authorities and agents of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation and London's Scotland Yard have scoured the area, using sniffer dogs brought from Germany and even digging up graves, but turned up no clues.
"We have had a few reports of people saying that they have been killed and that they are buried in a cave or thrown in a ditch," Julie Mangan said.
"But one man came out with three different accounts. Until we have proof positive, until we see with our own eyes, how can you believe that?"
Dirk Hasert's sister, Birgit Hasert, said: "It is very hard, but we can't give up. We have hope."
The three women hoped to meet senior Indian government officials in New Delhi before going to Srinagar to talk to police, separatist leaders and local citizens.
Schelly, from Spokane, Washington, planned to continue on to Islamabad where she hoped to see President Farooq Khan Leghari and Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif.
